beats.intro: Chapter two, lesson two. Simple proteins, and biological value. [[jelly]]Here is a gelatin dessert, a boiled egg, and a glass of milk. All three are protein, but they are not the same kind of protein, and they do not feed us equally well. [[tree]]Last lesson ended on a chain of amino acids, the root of our protein family tree. Today we light up the first branch, the simple proteins. Then we ask how good a protein is as food.
beats.types: [[root]]The lecture sorts proteins into three classes. [[simple]]Simple proteins are formed only of amino acids. Break one down by hydrolysis and you get amino acids, and nothing else. [[conj]]Conjugated, or compound, proteins are a protein plus a non-protein part. [[derived]]Derived proteins are products of the hydrolysis of simple or compound proteins. Lesson three adds the products of denaturation. [[lit]]Today we stay on the simple branch.
beats.simple: [[four]]The lecture's table lists four groups of simple proteins: albumin, globulin, histone, and the albuminoids, also called scleroproteins. The list also names protamine, glutelin and gliadin. We will only name those three, and meet gliadin again at the end. [[alb]]Albumin turns up in the egg, as egg albumin. In milk, as lactalbumin. And in blood, as serum albumin. [[glob]]Globulin has the same three homes: egg globulin, lactoglobulin in milk, and serum globulin in blood. [[heat]]Both are coagulated by heat. Coagulation is a change in the protein, from a liquid to a solid, or to a thicker liquid. [[egg]]Fry an egg, and the clear white turns solid and white. That is albumin coagulating.
beats.q1: Quick check. Which simple proteins are coagulated by heat?
beats.histone: [[hist]]Next, the histones. Histones are basic proteins, rich in basic amino acids. Remember the basic ones from chapter one: A, H, L. Arginine, histidine and lysine. [[dna]]Basic means positively charged, and that suits them to DNA, which carries negative charges. Histones sit with the nucleic acid and pack it into nucleosomes, like thread wound onto spools. [[not]]Unlike albumin and globulin, histones are not coagulated by heat.
beats.scler: [[hair]]Then the albuminoids, also called scleroproteins, the supporting proteins. Keratin makes hair and nail. [[coll]]Collagen is found in skin, in connective tissue, in tendon, and in bone. [[nots]]The lecture gives them four nots. Not coagulated by heat. Not digested by the usual enzymes. Not soluble in water. And not found in plants. [[sup]]Their job is support and protection. Boil an egg and it goes hard. Boil a fingernail, and nothing happens.
beats.gelatin: [[bone]]Now gelatin, marked with two stars on the slide. Boil bones and skin for a long time, and the collagen is turned into gelatin. [[gel]]Let it cool, and it sets into a gel. That is the jelly in the dessert. [[easy]]Gelatin is easily digested, unlike the collagen it came from. [[low]]But it is not an adequate diet. It has low biological value, because it lacks tryptophan, one of the essential amino acids. [[note]]One note. Gelatin is made from collagen by boiling, so many textbooks file it under derived proteins. The lecture lists it with the simple proteins, so learn it there, and remember that other answer too.
beats.q2: Quick check. Why does gelatin have a low biological value?
beats.value: [[ess]]Biological value tells us how completely a protein supplies the essential amino acids, the ones from chapter one that the body cannot make, and the diet must bring. [[high]]High biological value proteins contain all the essential amino acids. The lecture's examples are casein of milk, albumin, and globulin. [[low]]Low biological value proteins lack one or more of them: gelatin, gliadin, the protein of wheat, and vegetable proteins. [[veg]]Take that last one with care. Many plant proteins are short of an essential amino acid, but soy is complete, and a mix such as rice with beans fills each other's gaps. [[cas]]And casein, the milk protein, is also a phosphoprotein, which we meet in lesson three.
beats.sort: [[plate]]Let us use this on a plate. [[egg]]An egg gives albumin and globulin. Simple, coagulated by heat, high value. [[milk]]Milk gives casein, lactalbumin and lactoglobulin. High value. [[jel]]The jelly gives gelatin. Easily digested, but low value, with no tryptophan. [[bread]]Wheat bread gives gliadin. Low value, because it is short of at least one essential amino acid. [[mix]]So a good diet mixes its sources, so that what one food lacks, another supplies.
beats.wrap: To sum up. [[s1]]Simple proteins give only amino acids on hydrolysis. Albumin and globulin, from egg, milk and blood, are coagulated by heat. [[s2]]Histones are basic, and pack DNA into nucleosomes. [[s3]]Albuminoids, keratin and collagen, are the supporting proteins, with four nots. Gelatin, from boiled collagen, gels on cooling and is low in tryptophan. [[s4]]High value proteins carry every essential amino acid. Low value proteins lack one or more. [[end]]Now try the practice.
